name: Basaa (Ndog-Bacek)
overview: The Ndog-Bacek form the majority core of a Basaa group that has absorbed several neighbouring groups (Lìmùù, Liŋgɔ̀k, Mbamndân), who adopted Bàsàa. Settled on their ancestral land after a migration that set out from Ŋgɔk-Lituɓa, they live mainly from cocoa, the oil palm and bananas, in a patrilineal society where decisions are taken by consensus.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Central, majority group, part of a larger whole: the Lìmùù, Liŋgɔ̀k and Mbamndân have abandoned their own speech varieties there in favour of Bàsàa.
The same speech variety is found throughout the Nyong-et-Kéllé and, with little variation, in the Sanaga-Maritime.
The group is homogeneous but strictly practises exogamy: the Ndog-Bacek do not marry among themselves.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The group occupies its ancestral land, which belongs to it; the place has no particular religious value.
The migration set out from Ŋgɔk-Lituɓa, with a stopover at Mbɔgkanda-Maholo; no ties have been kept with these places.
According to tradition, the ancestors crossed the Sanaga by dugout canoe, and parts of that canoe are still kept.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Social organisation rests on caste and lineages.
Common decisions are taken behind closed doors, by consensus, among the representatives of each family line.
Interactions are open: society describes itself as very democratic.
A sub-clan alliance bond between brothers and sisters, called lìɓàba, structures solidarity.
Tensions with neighbours are defused by purification rites (Sày-Tuggwêt), so that there is no grudge inherited from history.
Rules of deference: a woman does not whistle or cross her legs in front of men; children kill the viper for the elders.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband's family, and frequent comings and goings to her parents are frowned upon.
One becomes a man by presenting one's fiancée to one's parents; one becomes a woman by presenting one's fiancé. No fixed age is imposed for marriage.
Steps: marriage proposal, bride price, then sealing of the union (ndombol likil).

The bride price comprises palm wine, kola, a goat and a wrapper: the wine erases the pains of upbringing and brings cheerfulness, the kola symbolises sharing and awakening, the goat “erases the blood” of the girl's birth, the wrapper places her family under honour.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The old cults (ancestors in November, sowing in March, harvests in February) are no longer practised.
Sacred site linked to water: Dipɓkɔɔɓôm, in Nkoumisé, on the bank of the river Lɔ̀bɛ́.
Birth is seen as the return of a forebear; death as a return to the ancestors, or as the fruit of human wickedness or of a punishment from the universe.
It is possible to get in touch with the spirit of the dead in difficult moments of life.
Major taboos: incest (likaa), murder (mbàk), eating a forbidden animal (cǒs). Serious offences (hitting one's parents, killing) are punished by quarantine.
Taboos: a man does not handle the cooking pots and must not damage the part of the palm that yields wine; a woman eats neither snail, nor viper, nor boa.
Divination: hìɓagi, hìtii, pàŋal, ŋgambi; oracles exist.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: cocoa growing, oil-palm groves, banana plantations, livestock rearing. Women: food crops (groundnut, cocoyam, cassava) and trade.
The land belongs to the men; it is accessed by inheritance, bequest or purchase according to customary law.
Ancestral crafts: fishing net (tan), bed (likondo), bench (koma), hunting lamp (pɛn), game bag (hikamba).

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Man's attire: wrapper, necklaces, boubou, hat; woman's: headscarf, earrings, wrapper, bracelets.
Traditional medicine remains widely used despite being disparaged.
Male ideal of beauty: strength and broad build; female: brown complexion, dimples, full figure.
Courtship: joviality, generosity, cleanliness and hard work in the man; cleanliness, hospitality and respect in the woman.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: hoŋgo, hisiko, mɓehla, ŋgola, diŋgɔma, makunɛ, bakalɛ, malɔŋgɛ.
Instruments: makwa, dikuu, ŋgɔm (drum), mandum, mandaŋ, miŋkeŋ, hiluŋ, makay.
Dances: mɓehla to welcome a new wife, hoŋgo for major celebrations, makunɛ and hisiko for rejoicing, malɔŋgɛ for rites, kɔɔ for funeral wakes.
No community festival specific to the group.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The Ndog-Bacek resemble the other “Ndog” groups (clothing, cooking, crafts).

sections.title: The names
items: Names indicate membership of the lineage: “hi ŋgon hi Njɔ̂k” for a boy, “ŋgɔ ŋgon hi Njɔ̂k” for a girl.
The name is given at the yayaa rite, on the 4th day for a girl and the 5th for a boy.
The name can change without limit (parents' wishes, circumstances).
The real name is avoided by means of pseudonyms and kinship terms: tâ (my father), ini (my mother), majo mǎn (little grandmother), sogol (grandfather).
The founding ancestor, Bacek (ɓa joy), bears a name with a double meaning: “let them exterminate” or “let them be exterminated”.

lessons.title: Who are the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition

vocabulary.frenchText: A place that is not easy to enter

lessons.competence: Introduce the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Central, majority group, part of a larger whole: the Lìmùù, Liŋgɔ̀k and Mbamndân have given up their own speech in favour of bàsàa. • The same speech variety is found throughout the Nyong-et-Kéllé and, with few variations, in the Sanaga-Maritime. • The group is homogeneous but strictly practises exogamy: the Ndog-Bacek do not marry among themselves. • The group occupies its ancestral land, which belongs to it; the place has no particular religious value. • The migration started from Ŋgɔk-Lituɓa, with a stop at Mbɔgkanda-Maholo; no ties have been kept with these places.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Ndog-Bacek form the majority core of a Basaa group that has absorbed several neighbouring groups (Lìmùù, Liŋgɔ̀k, Mbamndân), who adopted Bàsàa. Settled on their ancestral land after a migration that set out from Ŋgɔk-Lituɓa, they live mainly from cocoa, the oil palm and bananas, in a patrilineal society where decisions are taken by consensus.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment

vocabulary.langText: gâteau de manioc fermenté à l'huile rouge

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: nsugi (palm nut or groundnut sauce), ntɛgɛ̂ / mboŋgoo (black sauce), miŋkono (cucumber seed paste), mintoumba (fermented cassava cake with red oil), mpɛlɛ. • Drinks: palm wine (maɔk ma ŋgaŋ), raffia wine (maɔk ma dzâŋ). • Men: cocoa growing, oil palm plantations, banana plantations, livestock rearing. Women: food crops (groundnut, cocoyam, cassava) and trade. • Ancestral crafts: fishing net (tan), bed (likondo), bench (koma), hunting lamp (pɛn), game bag (hikamba).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) mainly eat nsugi, ntɛgɛ̂ / mboŋgoo, miŋkono, fermented cassava cake with red oil. Traditional drinks: maɔk ma ŋgaŋ, maɔk ma dzâŋ. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Marriage and bride price among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek)
objectives: Putting the stages of marriage in order
Explain the symbolism of the bride price
lessons.competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.
lessons.situation: Your elder brother wants to marry a young Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) woman. What steps will he have to follow?
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, props for the staging.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your older brother wants to marry a young Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) woman. Which steps will he have to follow?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who chooses the spouse? Do people marry within the group or outside it? — What are the stages of marriage? — What does the bride price include, and what does each item symbolise? — Where does the couple live after the marriage?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband's family, and frequent comings and goings to her parents' home are frowned upon. • One becomes a man by presenting one's fiancée to one's parents; one becomes a woman by presenting one's fiancé. No fixed age is required for marriage. • Stages: marriage request, bride price, then sealing of the union (ndombol likil). • The bride price comprises palm wine, kola, a goat and a wrapper: the wine erases the hardships of upbringing and brings cheer, the kola symbolises sharing and awakening, the goat “wipes away the blood” of the young woman's birth, the wrapper places her family under honour.

student.memo: Steps: marriage request, bride price, then sealing of the union (ndombol likil). The bride price includes palm wine, kola nut, goat and wrapper cloth: the wine erases the hardships of upbringing and brings joy, the kola nut symbolises sharing and awakening, the goat “wipes away the blood” of the girl's birth, the wrapper cloth places her family under honour.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek)
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares a Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and perform it.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) dance performance for cultural day.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Rhythms: hoŋgo, hisiko, mɓehla, ŋgola, diŋgɔma, makunɛ, bakalɛ, malɔŋgɛ. • Instruments: makwa, dikuu, ŋgɔm (drum), mandum, mandaŋ, miŋkeŋ, hiluŋ, makay. • Dances: mɓehla to welcome a new wife, hoŋgo for major celebrations, makunɛ and hisiko for festivities, malɔŋgɛ for rites, kɔɔ for funeral wakes. • No community festival specific to the group.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), traditional dances (mɓehla, hoŋgo, makunɛ) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: ŋgɔm, makwa, mandum, miŋkeŋ.

steps.instruction: Describe a Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Men: cocoa farming, palm groves, banana plantations, livestock. Women: food crops (groundnut, cocoyam, cassava) and trade. • Land belongs to men; it is accessed through inheritance, bequest or purchase according to customary law. • Ancestral crafts: fishing net (tan), bed (likondo), bench (koma), hunting lamp (pɛn), game bag (hikamba).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: cocoa growing, oil-palm groves, banana plantations, livestock rearing. Women: food crops (groundnut, cocoyam, cassava) and trade. Land belongs to men; it is acquired by inheritance, bequest or purchase according to customary law.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The old cults (ancestors in November, sowing in March, harvests in February) are no longer practised. • Sacred site linked to water: Dipɓkɔɔɓôm, at Nkoumisé, on the bank of the river Lɔ̀bɛ́. • Birth is seen as the return of an ancestor; death as a return to the ancestors, or as the result of human wickedness or a punishment from the universe. • It is possible to make contact with the spirit of the dead in difficult moments of life. • Major taboos: incest (likaa), murder (mbàk), eating a forbidden animal (cǒs). Serious offences (hitting one's parents, killing) are punished by quarantine.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The old cults (ancestors in November, sowing in March, harvests in February) are no longer practised. Sacred site linked to water: Dipɓkɔɔɓôm, in Nkoumisé, on the bank of the Lɔ̀bɛ́ river.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Bàsàa
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Bàsàa. • Greeting formulae: Mɛ nyega = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Mɛ nyega a = morning greeting (one person); Ma nyega bee = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Pɔk / yada, Iɓa, Iaa, Ina, Itan. • The founding ancestor, Bacek (ɓa joy), bears a name with a double meaning: “let them exterminate” or “let them be exterminated”. • The Ndog-Bacek resemble the other “Ndog” groups (clothing, cooking, crafts).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Bàsàa are the first steps towards communicating with the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Bàsàa.

activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Bàsàa are the first steps towards communicating with the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
